why: Is the lambda 0.9 spike a property or a lucky fit? ci-88 at lambda 0.9 is the only agent here that has beaten search-4 measurably (win rate 0.6550, interval 0.5988 to 0.7112) and it loses to Greedy 0.0325, so it is an exploit of one opponent and the gate refused it. ci-89 then walked to lambda 0.8 and refused the prediction written for it in both directions: better against Greedy (0.10375, not worse than 0.0325) and far worse against search-4 (0.27875, not better than 0.6625). So 0.9 is a peak against the teacher rather than a point on a trend -- nothing is monotone across 0.95, 0.9, 0.8 against either Greedy or search-4, and the only clean ordering is against Random, which is the opponent nobody is trying to beat. The stalling reading failed too: ci-89 plays search-4 nearly as long (16.7 rounds, 29.2% capped against ci-88's 17.1 and 38.2%) and scores 0.279 there, so reaching the round cap is not what wins those matches. This turn moves the dataset seed from 1 to 2 and puts lambda back to 0.9. The evaluation still uses the fixed benchmark seeds, so only the 1000 matches being fitted on change. If 0.6625 against search-4 survives a different draw, the spike is a property of that lambda against that teacher and is worth understanding; if it collapses, it was one lucky fit and three runs happened to point at noise. No prediction is written this time -- the last one earned none. Note the clone will not reproduce ci-69 on this run because its dataset changes too, which is expected and is not a regression. Still open: reading the capped matches apart from the decided ones, which is the measurement that would settle who is healthier at the cap rather than infer it; a second independent opponent that is not the teacher; and the nonlinear baseline ADR 0048 left on the table.
